bib.title: Artificial Artificial Artificial Intelligence: Crowd Workers Widely Use Large Language Models for Text Production Tasks

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Artificial Artificial Artificial Intelligence: Crowd Workers Widely Use Large Language Models for Text Production Tasks", Veniamin Veselovsky*, Manoel Horta Ribeiro*, Robert West (*equal contribution). Affiliation as printed: "EPFL" for all three. No venue is printed; the only identifier is "arXiv:2306.07899v1 [cs.CL] 13 Jun 2023", so preprint, 2023. The paper calls itself work in progress.

COVERAGE: 9 of 9 pages, 34,541 of 34,541 characters. Body is pp. 1-7, references pp. 7-9 (skimmed for origins). There are no appendices. All four figure captions and both tables were read.

CLAIMS

- claim: An estimated 33-46% of crowd-submitted summaries were produced with LLM help.
  number: 33-46%
  setup: 46 summaries from 44 MTurk workers, one abstract-summarisation task, around 1 June 2023. The range is two classifier thresholds, not one interval.
  quote: "we estimate that 21 of the 46 crowdsourced summaries (46%; 95% CI: [31%, 61%]) were synthetically generated" (logit threshold 0, p=50%); "using a threshold of 4 (corresponding to a predicted probability of 98%), we still arrive at an estimate of 15 of the 46 crowdsourced summaries (33%; 95% CI: [20%, 45%])"
  where: p5

- claim: The task was summarising NEJM medical abstracts (16 abstracts, about 400 words each) into at least 100 words, on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
  number: 48 summaries, 44 workers, 46 after de-duplication; 1 USD per summary, about 15 USD/hour
  setup: single summarisation step adapted from Horta Ribeiro et al. (2019); keystrokes and copy/paste logged with Javascript
  quote: "Workers were paid 1 USD per summary, which we estimate conservatively would take around 4 minutes to conclude, for a pay rate of 15 USD/hour. We obtained 48 summaries written by 44 distinct workers."
  where: p3

- claim: The detector is a fine-tuned e5-base classifier trained only on this task's data.
  number: 99% accuracy (summary-level split), 97% (abstract-level split)
  setup: real class = 16 original abstracts + 128 pre-LLM human summaries from the 2019 study; synthetic class = 320 ChatGPT summaries (10 per abstract at temperatures 0.7 and 1, prompted with the MTurk instruction). Held-out test data only, not the new MTurk responses.
  quote: Table 1: "Summary-level 0.99 ±0.02 0.99 ±0.03 0.99 ±0.02 0.98 ±0.04 / Abstract-level 0.97 ±0.03 0.97 ±0.02 0.97 ±0.02 0.97 ±0.04" (accuracy, macro-F1, precision, recall)
  where: p6 (data on p4)

- claim: Keystroke evidence is a post-hoc check, not part of the estimate.
  number: 41 of 46 summaries (89%) involved pasting; all 5 written without pasting were classified human; 15 synthetic were all pasted
  setup: conservative threshold of 4; assumes un-pasted text is human
  quote: "only five summaries were written entirely in the text box without any pasting. Importantly, our classifier labeled all of them as human-written"
  where: p6, Table 2

- claim: Summaries classified synthetic mostly had little overlap with the source abstract, suggesting the pasted text came from elsewhere.
  number: 10 of 13
  setup: pasted summaries with longest-common-substring overlap under 10%
  quote: "out of 13 summaries with an overlap of less than 10%, 10 (76%) were classified as synthetically generated"
  where: p6

- claim: Off-the-shelf detectors did poorly on this task.
  number: 6 of 10
  setup: 10 ChatGPT summaries the authors generated, tested on GPTZero
  quote: "out of 10 summaries that we had synthesized via ChatGPT, GPTZero detected only six as synthetic"
  where: p3

- claim (conclusion for crowd-label users): crowdsourced text can no longer be assumed to be a human gold standard, and crowd workers may shift to being a filter on model output.
  number: none
  quote: "the data would no longer be the intended human gold standard" (p1); "Instead of providing de novo annotations, crowd workers may instead serve as an important human filter for detecting when these models succeed and when they fail." (p7)

LIMITS
- No correction for classifier error was applied. You asked how it was corrected: it was not. The 33-46% is raw classified counts at two thresholds; each CI is a sampling interval on 46 items. The 5 un-pasted summaries are the only false-positive check, and the false-negative rate is only argued qualitatively.
- No ground truth for LLM use: no worker admitted or was observed using one. The keystroke logic rests on two stated assumptions.
- Authors concede one task only: "we acknowledge the uncertainty regarding the generalization of our findings to other tasks". It was chosen because it is easy for LLMs.
- Not shown: labelling or classification tasks (as opposed to text production), other platforms (Prolific, Upwork are named but not tested), worker qualifications or filters, quality of the LLM-assisted summaries, or any LLM other than ChatGPT in the training data.
- The 2019 human summaries and 2023 responses differ in more than LLM availability (worker pool, task variant), which the classifier could pick up.
- Dated: a June 2023 snapshot, v1. The promised update was not in this PDF.
- Minor arithmetic: 10/13 is 77%, printed as 76%.

BUILDS ON: Horta Ribeiro, Gligoric and West (2019), "Message distortion in information cascades" (task and human data); Wang et al. (2022), e5 embeddings (classifier); Suzgun et al. (2023), string2string (overlap measure).

CODE: none in the PDF. Repository printed: https://github.com/epfl-dlab/GPTurk

FIGURES: one candidate, Figure 1, p2: "Illustration of our approach for quantifying the prevalence of LLM usage among crowd workers solving a text summarization task." It shows the pipeline (pre-LLM human responses plus ChatGPT responses train the classifier, which is then applied to new MTurk responses, with keystrokes as a side check) faster than prose.

PROBLEMS: Extraction was clean. Figure 3 and 4 axis text is interleaved with body text but the captions are readable. No embedded instructions were found.
